newsitem.title: KENYA: Zairean rebels offer broad-based government-radio.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels offer broad-based government-radio.

text.p: Zairean rebels are offering to set up a broad-based national government excluding followers of President Mobutu Sese Seko but including Etienne Tshisekedi's opposition movement, rebel radio said on Wednesday.
The radio, broadcasting from the eastern town of Bunia, was quoted by the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs.

"Rebel radio...said the current parliament would be dissolved and a broad-based national unity government would be formed from which 'all Mobutists' will be excluded," the U.N. department said in a summary.
"Etienne Tshisekedi's Sacred Heart alliance would be given 'a defined place' within the government," it added.
"The newly formed government is required to take up the challenge left by Mr Mobutu and his decaying regime, to build up this country, which has been crushed to pulp," it said.

The role of other opposition groups has been an important element in talks on a transfer of power in Zaire from President Mobutu, who is sick with cancer and has lost control of most of the country to the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
At inconclusive talks with Mobutu at the weekend, rebel leader Laurent Kabila demanded the president hand over power to the rebel alliance immediately.
Mobutu refused, saying he would only hand power to a transitional authority which would then hold elections.

The United States has pressed Kabila to establish a transitional government that would include other political opponents as well as his rebel alliance. The ultimate goal is a democratic Zaire set up under free elections.
U.S. officials said this week that U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who has been touring the region, is pressing for "an inclusive transitional government leading to elections".

The United States is not insisting that Mobutu or his allies must be part of the arrangement but is suggesting that other elements of Zaire's political opposition, not just Kabila's forces, could be involved, U.S. officials said.
Diplomats at U.N. headquarters in New York say they are hoping Mobutu will resign and turn over power to parliament, which in turn could name someone to negotiate with Kabila.

"He (Kabila) would be an important player but he should not take over entirely," said one U.N. source. "There is a political class, a civil society that has to agree. You can't just tell Mobuto to give Kabila power and he takes over."
Mobutu left Kinshasa for Gabon on Wednesday for a summit meeting amid speculation that he may not return.
